12.3.5 The ICG 2026 report stated:

‘The election went ahead mostly smoothly, with few reports of violence or wrongdoing, marking a stark contrast with most polls in Bangladesh’s post-independence history …

‘Polling day itself went ahead with few reports of violence or malpractice… Several reasons lie behind the achievement of one the most peaceful elections in Bangladeshi history. The interim government and army both played important roles, including through close collaboration on security. The visible presence and proactive approach of security agencies helped defuse potential unrest and put voters at ease. Despite AL leaders’ insistence that the vote was undemocratic due to the party’s absence from the ballot sheet, they seemingly made little effort to disrupt it. Leaders of participating political parties, meanwhile, sought to restrain members …’[footnote 125]

12.3.6 The political analyst at an international NGO told the UK HO FFM team, when asked about violence during the 2026 election period, that:

‘There was no widespread political violence during the pre-election period. We promoted peaceful election processes across the parties. It was a realisation from opposition parties that if there was violence BNP, JeI etcetera would be the losers. We shared survey data with decision makers and campaign managers in political parties which found that 92% of people would not vote for a party engaged in violence. This enabled an understanding at grass roots levels.

‘We had a response system - if we suspected any violence was bubbling then we would contact the political parties to get them to internally resolve [the issue] …’[footnote 126]

12.3.7 The political analyst at an International NGO told the UK HO FFM team that ‘… because participating political parties did not want violence, it was one of the most peaceful election periods. Our interventions also helped to prevent political violence.’[footnote 127]

12.4 Election procedures

12.4.1 Regarding procedures on election day, the COG 2026 election report noted:

‘In all instances observed by our Group, ballot materials were distributed to polling stations in advance of the opening of polls. Polling staff followed pre-poll procedures in accordance with prescribed guidelines.

‘Polling stations opened on time. Opening procedures were implemented in a professional manner. Voting was conducted in a peaceful manner, with procedures largely followed. While a few isolated incidents were reported, these did not appear to affect the overall conduct of voting in a systemic manner …

‘Polling agents were observed in all polling stations. In general, they conducted themselves professionally throughout the voting process … The layout at polling stations ensured the secrecy of the ballot.

‘We observed the presence of police and other security officials in all polling stations. They were professional, and enabled an orderly and peaceful atmosphere. We observed the introduction of CCTV at polling stations, and body cameras on security personnel. These measures enhanced security, without compromising the integrity of the process.’[footnote 128]

12.4.2 An EU EOM February 2026 statement noted:

‘The election day was overall orderly, festive and calm, with competent polling staff efficiently facilitating voting in polling stations observed by the EU EOM …

‘Voting was orderly and professionally managed …

‘Counting was efficient in all EOM observations, but integrity safeguards were not uniformly implemented …

‘Results tabulation was transparent in all but three of the Mission’s 120 observations … The JeI and NCP publicly challenged results in several constituencies in Dhaka.’[footnote 129]

12.4.3 The AIIA March 2026 analysis article noted: ‘The election itself was administered competently. Voter turnout reached 59 percent, a significant increase from the previous parliamentary election, and Election Day was largely peaceful despite isolated incidents.’[footnote 130]

12.4.4 Regarding the counting of election ballots, the COG 2026 election report noted: ‘At the close of polls at 4:30 PM [12 February 2026], most polling stations we observed had no queues. We observed that polls generally closed on time and polling officials adhered to procedures. Our observers followed the results process, from polling stations to Returning Officers’ locations, in various constituencies. We observed the transparent nature of the count at polling stations, as well as the counting of postal ballots.’[footnote 131]

12.4.5 Regarding allegations of election tampering, on 13 February 2026, an Al Jazeera article reported:

‘Both the NCP and the BNP initially alleged irregularities and tampering with results, suggesting that some parties were benefitting from “election engineering”, though they provided limited specific evidence.

‘Jamaat also voiced its concern in a statement about the unofficial results, posted on its Facebook page.

‘“We are not satisfied with the process surrounding the election results. From candidates of the 11-party alliance [a Jel-led alliance, including the NCP[footnote 132]] narrowly and suspiciously losing in various constituencies, to repeated inconsistencies and fabrications in unofficial result announcements, the Election Commission’s reluctance to publish voter turnout percentages, and indications that a section of the administration leaned towards a major party – all of this undoubtedly raises serious questions about the integrity of the results process,” the statement said. However, on Saturday [14 February 2026], Jamaat’s Rahman conceded and said he would “serve as a vigilant, principled, and peaceful opposition”.’[footnote 133]

14.2.6 See also Security and anti-corruption efforts.

12. 2026 elections

12.1 Electoral reform

12.1.1 The BTI 2026 report noted:

‘Upon assuming power, the IG formed the so-called Election Reform Commission to ensure transparency and greater electoral fairness. It ultimately made more than 150 recommendations across 16 key areas. For example, legislation should be enacted to establish a permanent national constitutional council responsible for appointing members to constitutional bodies such as the Election Commission. The Election Commission should also be empowered to suspend or cancel elections in cases of malpractice, appoint its secretaries independently and, with unanimous approval, delay elections for up to 90 days during anticipated crises. Another recommendation was for the Election Commission to declare the credibility of elections within 48 hours of the results, enabling aggrieved parties to file appeals with the Constitutional Council or the Appellate Division. Lastly, a specialized cadre for Election Commission officials should be established to ensure professionalism and independence in election management.’[footnote 99]

12.1.2 Regarding co-operation between political parties and the interim government, the same report stated:

‘… In recent months … political parties, the interim government (IG) and reform commissions have begun working together to implement reforms to strengthen internal democracy, increase transparency in candidate selection and limit the influence of dynastic leadership. These efforts also include proposals to enforce mandatory internal elections, introduce campaign finance regulations and establish codes of conduct for party operations to ensure greater accountability and reduce factionalism.’[footnote 100]

12.1.3 In February 2026, International IDEA interviewed Md Abdul Alim, a member of the Electoral Reform Commission. The article noted that:

‘… the interim government has taken important steps to bolster the credibility of the upcoming election. He [Alim] states that “roughly 50 of the Electoral Reform Commission’s 250 recommendations have already been adopted into Bangladesh’s legal framework. These include strengthening the Election Commission’s administrative powers, provisions for overseas voting and measures to increase polling transparency.” Moreover, the law now bans party figures from remaining inside polling stations throughout the voting process (previously a common practice …), giving the presiding officer authority to remove and take legal actions against them.

‘While these changes improve past electoral management practices, Alim notes that many electoral reforms remain pending, such as the independent appointment of election commissioners, among broader proposals in the July Charter.’[footnote 101]

12.1.4 For information on other reforms proposed by the IG, see Legislative, constitutional and policy reform.

12.2 Political participation

12.2.1 On 25 December 2025, BBC News reported:

‘Tarique Rahman, the front-runner to be the next prime minister of Bangladesh, has returned to the country after 17 years in exile ahead of landmark general elections… Rahman’s return comes in the wake of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina being ousted last year.

‘He had been the subject of various criminal investigations launched while her Awami League party was in power but was cleared of all charges when her regime fell.’[footnote 102]

12.2.2 The EU EOM April 2026 report stated: ‘On 11 December 2025, the Bangladesh Election Commission (EC) announced that parliamentary elections would be held on 12 February 2026, concurrently with a referendum on the July National Charter.’[footnote 103]

12.2.3 In relation to voter registration, the EU EOM 2026 report noted:

‘… more than 127.7 million voters registered for these elections, an increase of 8 million compared with the January 2024 poll …

‘Under the active registration system, eligible citizens must apply to be included on the lists …The voter lists closed on 31 October 2025, with voters who turned 18 before that date being eligible for inclusion. The completeness and accuracy of voter lists was assessed positively by most EU EOM interlocutors …’[footnote 104]

12.2.4 Regarding political party campaigning, the same report noted:

‘The campaign was pluralistic, dynamic and competitive, and voters were presented with a wide choice of distinct political agendas. Fundamental freedoms of assembly and expression were generally respected. While political parties were overall able to compete on a level playing field, in some constituencies some candidates benefited from close links with district or local authorities, as well as unequal access to financial resources. Of the 50 contesting parties, only four conducted nationwide campaigns, with the BNP and JeI being most visible, and the IAB [Islami Andolan Bangladesh] and NCP present to a lesser extent. Candidates relied on a wide range of campaign methods, including outdoor advertising, in-person events, street campaigning, and digital outreach. Senior party figures, such as BNP’s Tarique Rahman and JeI’s Shafiqur Rahman, led high-profile rallies attended by tens of thousands and followed live on Facebook by over 40 million viewers each. The EU EOM observed 190 in-person campaign events, most of which were peaceful, and had adequate police protection, although confrontational rhetoric emerged at times. In the digital space, official party and candidate pages were primarily used for self promotion, while unofficial supporting accounts were often used for attacking opponents. The tone of the campaign hardened closer to elections, with parties frequently accusing each other of creating an uneven playing field, and of threats and violence.’[footnote 105]

5.1.6 The newly elected BNP government reviewed the ordinances made under the interim government related to reform and, although they have allowed some to lapse, they have converted most into law, including changes to the Code of Criminal Procedure to safeguard against arbitrary arrest. Some of the lapsed ordinances have subsequently been re-drafted and admitted into law such as the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Bill, and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) Bill. These were passed in parliament on 7 September 2026, with some criticism from the opposition and civil society organisations, who considered them to provide weaker protections than the IG’s ordinances. Several sources told the UK Home Office Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) in June 2026 that progress on implementing the July Charter and broader reform recommendations has been limited, but many also acknowledged that it was still early in the new government’s tenure (see Reform of the security forces and judiciary and Reform agenda of the BNP government).

5.1.7 Sources indicate that concerns about politically motivated policing had reduced under the newly elected BNP government compared to the period of AL rule. Police representatives told the Home Office FFM team that all individuals, regardless of political affiliation, can access police protection and assistance, and that an individual can issue a complaint to police officials or the courts if they believe that police have not responded appropriately to their case. Non-governmental organisations also indicated that access to police protection is less politicised than during the AL government and that members and supporters of the political opposition are able to access police protection (see Conduct of law enforcement personnel).

5.1.8 Hundreds of senior officials and AL leaders under the former government have been arrested and remanded into custody in relation to deaths that occurred during the July/August 2024 protests and criminal acts that took place during the AL’s tenure in government. Other cases have been instigated against mayors, law enforcement personnel, and members of AL auxiliary organisations. Trials against those arrested are ongoing. The government has a legitimate right to act against criminal acts and to use all lawful and proportionate means to do so, including against those involved in criminal acts during the former regime and the protests (see Arrest and prosecution of Awami League members and affiliates under the interim government, Arrest and prosecution of Awami League members and affiliates under the BNP government, Accountability for corruption and abuses committed under the Awami League government).

5.1.9 For further guidance on assessing state protection, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

6. Internal relocation

6.1.1 Where the person has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from the state, they are unlikely to be able to internally relocate to escape that risk.

6.1.2 Where the person has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a non-state or rogue state actor, due to their actual or perceived political opinion, they are likely to be able to internally relocate to escape that risk. This is because in general, there are parts of country, such as (but not limited to) Dhaka, where it will be reasonable to expect them to relocate.

6.1.3 Bangladesh is a large country with a population of over 177 million people. Dhaka is the most populous city in Bangladesh, with a large urban population of 23.21 million people. For further information, and consideration of the reasonableness of internal relocation generally, see the Country Policy and Information Note Bangladesh: Internal relocation.

6.1.4 For consideration of internal relocation for women, see also the Country Policy and Information Note on Bangladesh: Women fearing GBV.

6.1.5 Members of the political opposition can, in general, internally relocate within Bangladesh. Leaders, members and supporters of the AL, who have had problems within their local communities, have relocated to other districts within Bangladesh following the July/August 2024 uprising, and some have returned to their home areas following the February 2026 general election (see Awami League and affiliates).

6.1.6 Low-level AL members, particularly those who have joined or reached understandings with other political parties, and those who are not publicly associated with corruption or human rights abuses committed under the previous AL government, do not generally face harassment in areas of relocation (see Awami League and affiliates).

6.1.7 Higher-profile AL members, particularly those accused of corruption or human rights abuses during the period of AL rule are likely to face adverse public attention. Sources reported that high-profile AL members had gone into hiding, but a representative of a Bangladeshi human rights organisation advised that such individuals would be more likely to be handed over to the police than subjected to violence in the community (see Awami League and affiliates, Risk, Protection).

6.1.8 For further guidance on internal relocation and factors to consider, see the Asylum Instruction on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

7. Certification

7.1.1 Where a claim from an actual or perceived BNP affiliate, supporter, member or leader, based on a fear of the state or non-state/rogue-state actors, is refused, it is likely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.
